objectives.text: Distinguish canon, institutional teaching, commentary, and historical evidence.
State a doctrinal claim with a source and a limit.

questions.title: What kind of source is this?
questions.prompt: Classify the evidence in each example. Classify the named source itself, rather than every statement it might quote.
questions.instructions: Match each statement on the left to exactly one answer on the right. Use every answer once.

leftItems.text: The text of Article of Faith 4 in the Pearl of Great Price
A current Church-published explanation of a gospel topic
A dated personal diary reporting what its writer heard in 1880
An author’s interpretation in a devotional book, with no identified institutional endorsement

questions.explanation: These categories describe evidentiary roles rather than a universal ranking. Scripture, institutional explanation, historical reporting, and individual interpretation are different source types; an excerpt quoted inside a source should be evaluated separately.
questions.perspective: Latter-day Saint institutional / Original Hearken teaching method

presentation.accessibility: Every pair must be selectable, announceable, changeable, and clearable without dragging.

questions.title: Find the Article of Faith
questions.prompt: Match each summary to the article that explicitly addresses it.
questions.instructions: Match each statement on the left to exactly one answer on the right. Use every answer once.

leftItems.text: Belief in the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
Punishment for personal sins rather than Adam’s transgression
Salvation through Christ’s Atonement and obedience to gospel laws and ordinances
Faith in Jesus Christ, repentance, baptism by immersion for remission of sins, and laying on of hands for the gift of the Holy Ghost

questions.explanation: Each summary follows the corresponding article. Knowing which text supports a claim helps learners attribute it accurately without treating these four summaries as an exhaustive theology.

sources.title: Sources, authority, and careful claims
sources.body: Studying doctrine begins with identifying the kind of claim being made. A passage can be canonical, a statement can represent current institutional teaching, and a book can offer useful commentary without all three having the same function. A historical record may tell us what someone taught at a particular time without settling what the Church teaches today. Keep four fields beside every note: claim, source, setting, and confidence. Ask whether your wording is broader than the evidence. “This passage teaches…” is often more defensible than “Every Latter-day Saint believes…”. This course assesses your ability to understand and explain teachings; it does not assess personal belief or religious worthiness. Start a source ledger now. You will revise it as new evidence changes how precisely you can express a claim.
